transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-25 11:00 PST / 19:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees:
 - Alex Kim (Redwood, AE)
 - Priya Desai (Redwood, SE)
 - Jordan Lee (Redwood, CSM)
 - Michael Lopez (Enumera, CTO)
 - Sara Chen (Enumera, ML Platform Lead)
 - David Park (Enumera, Security)
 - Anita Ruiz (Enumera, Eng Manager)

Summary: Quick migration demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Walkthrough of API equivalence, streaming/func-calls parity, embeddings and rerank mapping, cost/latency considerations, and next steps for a pilot and benchmarks.

Topics: parity mapping, API differences, streaming & function calling, embeddings compat, KV/prefix cache, latency vs cost, private deployment requirements (VPC/KMS), Redwood Console observability, Redwood Optimize recommendations.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you all making time. Quick roll call — I'm Alex, AE on the Redwood infra team, Priya's gonna run the demo, Jordan's here for CSM stuff. Michael — over to you for a sec?
[00:18] Michael: Hey Alex, yeah thanks, we got the core team here. Sara, David, Anita. We're excited to see how the migration looks — mostly concerned about parity with our existing OpenAI and Together flows, plus compliance stuff.
[00:34] Priya: Great, cool. I'll share my screen in a sec, just to set expectations: we'll show API request/response mapping, streaming and function/tool calling, embeddings mapping, and then touch on Console and Optimize. Hoping to leave time for Q&A and concrete next steps.
[00:49] Anita: Sounds good. We have a pretty mixed stack — some endpoints hit OpenAI for chat completion, others use Anthropic for safety-first responses, and we started a POC with Together for some tuned models.
[01:05] Priya: Perfect, that's actually a common pattern. When we talk parity mapping, there are three levels: 1) request/response surface — how you call the API, params and model names; 2) behavior parity — temperature/top-p/stop tokens and function calling semantics; 3) infra parity — latency, KV cache, quantized runtimes, and autoscaling.
[01:25] Sara: On behavior parity, function calling is a big one for us, our orchestration relies on structured tool calls. Does Redwood support the same pattern?
[01:34] Priya: Yes — Redwood has first-class function/tool calling; the request schema is slightly different but we provide a drop-in SDK mapping and an example parity layer. You can keep your existing JSON schemas — we translate them server-side and map to Redwood's structured call format.
[01:48] Michael: Are there any gotchas? Like differences in how Anthropic handles safety or Together handles prompt tokens?
[01:57] Priya: Good question. There are two common gotchas: prompts and system message handling — Anthropic's prompt format sometimes injects guardrails differently — and token accounting. We'll show a parity example.
[02:12] Priya: (screen: code sample) Here is an OpenAI-style chat call. On the left is the original request to openai.com/v1/chat/completions, and on the right is the Redwood equivalent: model name mapping (we map openai:gpt-4 -> redwood/gpt4-compat), messages mapping, and a small adapter that handles function/call routing.
[02:32] Alex: Note that our model catalog includes verified compatibility profiles — we publish lat/throughput numbers for common seq lengths so you can pick the right variant.
[02:42] Sara: Does that mean if we pick redwood/gpt4-compat, it's identical output to OpenAI's GPT-4?
[02:49] Priya: Not identical — compatibility, meaning same API contract and similar behavior for many prompts, but there will be model-specific differences. For strict behavioral parity we recommend tying evals to your sample prompt set and enabling Redwood Optimize to surface regression alerts.
[03:04] David: From security, we need to understand what stays in our VPC, and where logs live. We can't have PHI go to a third-party without controls.
[03:12] Alex: Totally. We have Redwood Private and Dedicated options. With Private, the control plane is customer-managed and you can run the model-serving plane inside your VPC or on-prem. Audit logs, KMS integration, and SOC 2 scope are supported — we'll send the security pack.
[03:27] Priya: Back to parity — here's an example of function calling. (screen) On OpenAI you send functions array and the model may choose to call. Redwood supports the same flow; our SDK exposes a callResult structure. One caveat: when streaming is enabled, we stream tokens and function-calling decisions as events — there can be a small mapping layer if you need exactly the same event shapes.
[03:52] Michael: Streaming is critical for our chat latency SLA. How do your streams compare?
[03:59] Priya: For hosted API we support chunked transfer / server-sent events similar to OpenAI streaming. For Dedicated we can tune the runtime to reduce token latency via continuous batching and lower-latency kernel selection — basically we optimize for the distribution you provide.
[04:17] Anita: You mentioned KV cache — can we reuse conversation context across calls like a local cache?
[04:24] Priya: Yes, we have KV/prefix caching that stores key-value attention caches for recurrent contexts — reduces cost and latency for multi-turn scenarios. For some models the cache format differs, so the adapter manages cache keys.
[04:36] Sara: Ok, show us embeddings — we have a rerank pipeline using Anthropic embeddings currently.
[04:42] Priya: (screen: embeddings sample) Redwood exposes an embeddings endpoint that's directly compatible: you send a text array and get back vectors. We also provide a rerank helper and pretrained index examples. Note: vector dims and normalization may differ slightly between vendors — we include conversion utilities in the SDK.
[04:59] Michael: Cost — we need unit cost comparisons. We saw your published numbers but need to map them to our token mix.
[05:07] Alex: We'll run a parity cost analysis in the spreadsheet — we'll need your token distribution. Priya can run a representative benchmark; Redwood Optimize will also recommend batching/quantization profiles for cost savings.
[05:20] Priya: Quick demo of the console: (screen) here's per-model latency breakdown, token-level cost charts, and the rollout page where you can define canary policies. You can route requests by policy (region, tier) and fallback to a cheaper variant if SLOs are missed.
[05:39] Jordan: One practical tip: customers often start with Hosted to iterate fast, then move critical traffic to Dedicated when they need throughput guarantees or data isolation.
[05:49] David: For Dedicated or Private, what's the uptime SLA? We need 99.9 for some endpoints.
[05:56] Alex: Our Dedicated offering includes SLA options; we can discuss the exact number in contract talks. Private deployments can be configured with your infra SLAs and we provide monitoring hooks.
[06:07] Anita: Any friction porting existing code? We have a few edge cases where we rely on vendor-specific behavior like stop sequences and tokenization quirks.
[06:18] Priya: Yep — tokenization is a frequent source of small diffs. We provide a tokenizer compatibility layer and a parity test harness so you can run your prompt set and surface any output regressions. It's part of the migration playbook.
[06:33] Sara: Show us the parity spreadsheet example?
[06:37] Priya: (screen) This sheet maps OpenAI/Anthropic/Together API fields to Redwood fields. Example: openai.temperature -> temperature, openai:max_tokens -> max_tokens, together:top_p -> top_p, anthropic:system_message -> system_prompt (adapter normalizes). We also list model mappings like openai:gpt-4-ish -> redwood/gpt4-compat, anthropic:claude-2 -> redwood/claude2-compat, together:toozie-small -> redwood/together-small-compat (these names are illustrative).
[07:04] Michael: OK that helps. What about telemetry during a migration? We want to compare response distributions and failure modes.
[07:12] Priya: Redwood Console gives per-route histograms, sample outputs, and an evals dashboard. You can upload prompts and get side-by-side diffs across model variants. For regressions we can set alerts that trigger a lookback and optionally route to fallback models.
[07:28] David: On compliance, KMS integration — do you support customer-managed keys?
[07:33] Alex: Yes, KMS and HSM integrations are supported in Private. For Hosted we support encryption at rest and we can integrate with key rotation via our enterprise plan — again we'll send the security pack with specifics.
[07:47] Priya: Next I'm going to demo a short code parity example for a streaming function call, and then show an example of running a benchmark job in the Console.
[07:57] (screen) Priya: Code sample: here's a streaming chat call with functions. You open a websocket or SSE, you get token events and then a final function call event. The adapter ensures your existing orchestration that expects function-json still works.
[08:16] Sara: The SSE event shape — will we need to rework our orchestration layer?
[08:21] Priya: Minimal. The SDK has a compatibility payload that re-emits events in the OpenAI shape. Most customers use that for a quick swap.
[08:31] Michael: Performance — can we do a head-to-head on our real workload?
[08:35] Priya: Absolutely. That's the recommended pilot: provide prompts, traffic shape, and we run a benchmark on Hosted and on Dedicated config (if you want) to measure latency and throughput. We then produce a cost/latency tradeoff table and Optimize suggestions.
[08:50] Anita: How long does that take?
[08:52] Priya: Typically 1–2 weeks to run repeatable benchmarks and analysis depending on queue and sample size.
[08:58] Jordan: We'll propose a pilot plan in the follow-up: scope, duration, success criteria.
[09:04] David: A few more security questions: SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit log retention — do you provide granular RBAC?
[09:11] Alex: Yes — RBAC for routes/models, SSO/SAML for console, and configurable audit log retention. We'll include these details in the security pack.
[09:21] Priya: Demo: Console benchmark job — here's the job config where you point to a prompt file, set concurrency, and choose models. The results page shows P50/P95 latency, token counts, and a per-prompt diff view.
[09:36] Sara: That diff view will be important for us. We need to validate that certain prompts used in clinical summarization remain within quality thresholds.
[09:44] Priya: Totally understood. For clinical prompts we recommend running both functional tests and human evals; Redwood Optimize can wire human eval workflows and attach regression alerts.
[09:55] Michael: One more practical — what SDKs/languages do you support? Our stack is Python + Node.
[10:01] Alex: Official SDKs for Python, Node, and a simple REST shim. Most customers can switch quickly. We also have a migration guide and sample microservice.
[10:10] Anita: Any porting issues with tokenization again — do you have a tokenizer API?
[10:15] Priya: We expose tokenizer endpoints and local tokenizers in the SDK so you can run exact token accounting pre-flight.
[10:22] Michael: On model naming — how do you keep a stable name across model updates?
[10:27] Alex: We have pinned model versions and version aliases. You can pin a deployment to a version and then roll forward with canaries via the console.
[10:36] Sara: Great. Can you show us a real-world parity diff quickly?
[10:40] Priya: (screen) Example: prompt A — on OpenAI GPT-4 we get X, on Redwood/gpt4-compat we get X' — small phrasing differences. The eval framework highlights token-level diffs and we can add a remapping rule if you need identical formatting.
[10:57] David: Are logs PII redacted? For hosted mode, we need to ensure PHI isn't stored.
[11:03] Alex: For hosted, logs are retained but can be configured to redact or not store payloads containing PHI. For private it's under your control. We'll include the exact retention and redaction knobs.
[11:16] Priya: Ok wrapping into practical next steps: we'll send the parity mapping sheet and quickstart repo; Sara will share the prompt set; we'll run an initial benchmark and then do a follow-up to review results and pilot scope.
[11:28] Michael: Sounds good. Any pricing ballpark?
[11:31] Alex: We'll include a starter pricing spreadsheet based on estimated tokens and options for Hosted vs Dedicated. For Dedicated we can do reserved capacity pricing.
[11:40] Anita: If we start with Hosted and then go Dedicated, is that a big migration?
[11:45] Priya: Not huge. The API layer remains the same; the main changes are infra config and possibly a switch in model endpoint names. We help manage the rollout with canaries and traffic-shaping.
[11:56] Sara: One last ask — can you add an example of our reranker pipeline using Redwood embeddings to the repo?
[12:01] Priya: Yes, we'll add a rerank example and a small Dockerized microservice you can drop into your stack.
[12:07] Jordan: I'll follow up with a proposed pilot scope and calendar.
[12:12] Michael: Great, thanks everyone.
